extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal guidance on (1) when and how injunctions and attachments issue and are enforced in patent suits (including defenses and penalties for contempt), and (2) the equitable rules for ascertaining and recovering an infringer's profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decree protecting defendant's customers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the final decree allows the defendant to continue to make the articles in question free from interference from the plaintiff, it is proper that the decree also enjoin the plaintiff from bringing further suits against the defendant's customers, except when a decree in another circuit holding the patent valid and infringed has been affirmed by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of such a protective provision is proper but limited by prior affirmed decisions in other circuits; include explicit language in the decree to restrain plaintiff from suing customers when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful notices to customers by plaintiff allowed; misleading notices not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will issue on behalf of a defendant against a plaintiff in an infringement suit to restrain the latter from sending circulars to defendant's customers giving notice of the suit, and warning them against contributory infringement where the statements in the circulars are true and sent out in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sending truthful, good-faith notices is permitted. However, sending misleading notices or exaggerated statements of the scope and effect of the injunction which are calculated to injure the defendant's legitimate business will not be tolerated and may afford ground for dissolving the injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay of defendant's suit pending issuance of patent under Section 4915
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will also issue on application of a plaintiff in a suit to compel the issuance of a patent under Section 4915 of the Revised Statutes, to stay a suit brought by the defendant to enjoin infringement of the patent, until the suit under Section 4915 has been decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may stay defendant's enforcement suits pending resolution of administrative or statutory proceedings to compel patent issuance; apply where statutory procedure is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of injunctions in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless a writ is expressly made to apply to the use or sale, after the expiration of the patent, of specimens of the patented thing which were made before that time, such injunction cannot continue after that expiration; and surely no such writ will be made to apply to such use or sale of unpatented parts of an infringing combination. Indeed, no injunction ought in any case to continue after the expiration of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions normally terminate with the patent term. If extending post-expiration relief is sought, the decree must expressly state it and be narrowly tailored (e.g., to specimens made before expiration). Permanent/perpetual injunction language is misleading in patent context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's in personam decree power limited by patent territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: The court having acquired jurisdiction over the persons of the defendants may control them by decree in personam from doing any act within or without the jurisdiction which shall be an interference with the plaintiff's rights. Since the monopoly of a patent extends only to the territorial limits of the United States this power would not permit the court to enjoin the bringing of a suit on a foreign patent for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts can bind named defendants globally by personal decree, but cannot purport to control foreign patents or foreign suits because patent rights are territorial to the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment for contempt: required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An attachment will issue to bring an enjoined defendant before the court for punishment whenever the complainant institutes proper proceedings therefor, and proves that the defendant was promptly served with a writ of injunction, and that the writ contained a concise description of the particular thing, all specimens of which it forbade the defendant to make, use, or sell, and that the defendant did make, or use, or sell, or did cause to be made, used, or sold a specimen of that thing, or of a thing clearly the same, after having been served with that writ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before issuing attachment for contempt, establish timely service, sufficiently specific injunction terms, and affirmative proof of post-service disobedience. The description in the injunction must be sufficiently concise to identify the prohibited subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment against persons connected with defendant and corporate officers
rubrics_metrics.description: An attachment will likewise issue against any person who was connected with the defendant in defending against the suit, before the injunction was issued, and who was also connected with the defendant in disobeying that injunction, after he was informed of its issue; where the defendant is a corporation and an officer upon whom the writ was served was privy to its violation, an attachment will issue against him in person; an injunction duly served on a corporation is binding on all persons acting for that corporation, and who have notice of the writ and of its contents, whether they were actually served or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals who participated in defense and later disobey the injunction, and corporate officers privy to violation, may be attached. An injunction against a corporation binds those acting for it with notice. However, do not issue attachments against strangers merely because they succeeded to the business, absent collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on attachment for successors, strangers, and former employees
rubrics_metrics.description: An attachment will not issue against a stranger to the suit merely because he has succeeded to the business in the conduct of which the defendant infringed, except in cases where the stranger is acting in collusion with the defendant to help him avoid the injunction; and an attachment will not issue against one who was an employee of the defendant at the time of the issuance of the injunction but who has since engaged in an independent business in which he makes the articles adjudged to be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue contempt attachments against successor business owners or former employees who independently continue business unless collusion or other indicia make them liable; such cases call for independent suits rather than attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign sales of pre-existing articles not contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the thing proved to have been done by the enjoined defendant consists in sending to some foreign country, and selling there, articles which were made in the United States, in infringement of the patent, before the injunction was granted, an attachment will not issue, because such a transaction is not a violation of an injunction against the infringement of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales abroad of articles made prior to injunction generally do not constitute contempt of a U.S. injunction; analyze timing and whether conduct was within the injunction's prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not decide doubtful infringement on summary contempt proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: An attachment will not issue where the character of the defendant's doings, after the injunction, is doubtful. Doubtful questions will not be decided on summary proceedings to punish persons for contempt of court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the question of whether post-injunction acts infringe is doubtful, the proper remedy is a hearing on the merits (supplementary decree or new suit), not summary attachment for contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court duty on hearing motion for attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the court, on a hearing of a motion for an attachment, to examine what the defendant is proved to have done, and to issue an attachment if his doings satisfactorily appear, in the eye of the law, to constitute disobedience of the writ of injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge must weigh evidence of conduct; issue attachment only where the proof shows clear disobedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to limit injunction cannot be used to anticipate attachment motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for an attachment cannot be anticipated and outflanked by a motion to expressly limit the injunction, so as to exclude the doings of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural attempts to pre-empt attachment by narrowing the injunction should not be used to deprive the court of contempt enforcement; courts should consider both motions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment proceedings are independently reviewable
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for an attachment for contempt of court for violating an injunction is an independent criminal case, which can be taken to the Circuit Court of Appeals for review on a writ of error, while the action in equity out of which it arose, is still pending and progressing in the lower court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contempt/attachment proceedings have independent appellate rights; expect separate review pathways from the underlying equity action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defenses to attachment normally insufficient but relevant to intent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no defence to a motion for an attachment to show that the decision in pursuance of which the injunction was granted was wrong; or that new evidence has since been discovered which would have caused a contrary decision; or that the defendant was advised by counsel that his doings did not violate the injunction; although the fact that the defendant was acting under such advice will be considered in determining whether or not there has been intentional disregard of the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits challenges to the underlying decree are generally not an available defense in contempt proceedings, but subjective intent (e.g., reliance on counsel) may mitigate penalty; still, disobedience cannot be justified by counsel advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other fact-based excuses addressed but do not absolve disobedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Other factors—such as that what the defendant did was done as the employee of another; that the defendant merely ordered his employees not to sell the infringing articles without more energetic steps to enforce orders; or that the writ of injunction was for a while suspended in its operation by the consent of the complainant—are relevant but do not permit disobedience while the writ remains unchanged. If the writ was inadvertently made broader than the decision, the defendant may apply to correct it, but must not disobey it meanwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural or operational excuses may be considered in mitigation but generally do not permit open disobedience; seek court correction rather than self-help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of set-aside of consent decree
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an injunction was based on a consent decree entered in pursuance of a compromise of the parties, an attachment will not issue for a disregard of that injunction if that compromise has been set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction, or if such a court has enjoined the complainant from enforcing the contract of compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the consent basis for an injunction has been judicially undone, contempt attachments for violation of that injunction are improper; examine status of underlying decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for violation of injunctions vary with culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it appears that the defendant had no intention to disobey the writ, the penalty may be confined to an enforced payment of the costs of the motion for an attachment. Where the defendant had no intention but imprudently did so, the penalty may include the costs and a small fine. Where the disobedience is less excusable, the defendant may be compelled to pay all the expenses and counsel fees incurred by the complainant. And where disobedience of an injunction is excuseless and defiant, the penalty may be a reasonable fine and a reasonable imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate punishments to culpability: from costs to fines and imprisonment. Document intent and excuse carefully when arguing mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil v. criminal character of contempt punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the punishment imposed in a civil proceeding for contempt is by way of punitive fine or imprisonment it must appear that the defendant has failed to do something affirmatively required of him by the court's order. This situation seldom occurs in injunctions relating to patent rights (where the order is usually to desist); when a party has done an act which was forbidden, punitive fines/imprisonment are properly imposed only in criminal contempt proceedings (i.e., before a jury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish remedial civil sanctions (for affirmative enforcement) from punitive criminal contempt; when punitive sanctions are sought for forbidden acts, ensure criminal contempt procedures are followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary civil relief for contempt where it remedies injury
rubrics_metrics.description: By reason of the violation of an injunction by doing forbidden acts, the contempt may be productive of injury to the other party and to the extent that that injury may be remedied by the payment of money, the offending party may be compelled in a civil proceeding to reimburse the opposite party for the latter's expenses of the contempt proceeding and for the damage caused by the violation of the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the harm from contempt is compensable in money, pursue civil reimbursement (expenses, damages) even if punitive sanctions require criminal contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverable profits: actual profits from the infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The profits which are recoverable in equity for the infringement of a patent, are those which the defendant made from that infringement. They are the profits which he actually made; not those which with worse, or better, management he would or might have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain actual realized profits attributable to the infringement; hypothetical profits are not recoverable. If a particular infringer realized no profit from his infringement, none can be recovered from him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverable profits must be direct results of the infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The recoverable profits are those which resulted directly, and do not include any which resulted indirectly, from the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude downstream, market-wide indirect effects (e.g., price increases to unrelated product lines) that are not direct profits of the infringing act; use proximate-cause analysis (Piper v. Brown example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of profits among joint infringers and successive owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several defendants were joint infringers of a patent, but where all the resulting profits were received by part of the wrongdoers, the decree for profits will be rendered only against those defendants who realized them. Successive owners of an infringing business transferred pendente lite are each liable only for the profits made by himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate liability for profits to those who actually realized them; apportion profits over time according to participation and ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profitable and unprofitable infringements treated separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a part of the infringement of a defendant resulted in profits, and the residue resulted in losses, the complainant is entitled to recover those profits without any deduction on account of those losses. Each infringement is treated by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not offset profitable infringement recoveries by separate loss-making activities; analyze each infringing act or contract discretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of account of profits
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits cannot be had where none arose before the action was begun, but such an account is not confined to those which accrued before the interlocutory decree was entered, but may be made to include all profits realized by the defendant from infringing the complainant's right, at any time prior to the closing of the account. And such an account will be taken in conformity with the statutes relevant thereto, as they existed at the respective dates when the infringement occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims for an account should cover all defendant profits from infringement up to the closing of the account, applying the law and statutes in effect at the time of each infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic rule: treat the infringer as trustee; evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The generic rule for ascertaining the amount of the profits recoverable in equity for the infringement of a patent, is that of treating the infringer as though he were a trustee for the patentee, in respect of the profits which he realized from his infringement. The specific rules are somewhat numerous and somewhat elastic. They all require the best evidence of which the nature of each particular case will reasonably admit, and that evidence must be reasonably definite and convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply trustee-equitable principles; adapt specific methods to the invention and circumstances; demand the best attainable, reasonably definite and convincing evidence when proving profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's royalty is not a measure of defendant's profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee's royalty is no measure of the defendant's profits, even in a case where the patentee habitually exercised his exclusive right by granting licenses to others. Nor are any other facts which relate to the measure of the complainant's damages material to inquiries touching the amount of the defendant's profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate a typical license royalty or patentee damages measure with the defendant's actual profits; measure profits independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits often computed as receipts minus cost of making and selling
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the amount it cost the defendant to make and sell his specimens of the patented thing, and the amount which he received for those specimens, is in many cases the amount of his profits. That is the fact where the only infringement consisted of such making and selling, and where no part of ascertainable cost or value, other than those covered by the patent in suit, entered into the composition of the specimens which were made and sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When infringement is limited to making/selling the patented articles, compute profits as sales revenue less properly allocated manufacturing and selling costs; collect direct cost evidence attributable to those specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: When separation of patented and unpatented contributions is impossible, whole profits may be recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent did not cover all the elements of the articles made and sold by the defendant, defendants who mingled profits made as an infringer with those made otherwise, and where there is no criterion by which they can be separated, must submit to the recovery of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant's conduct prevents reliable apportionment between patented and unpatented components, courts may award the entire profit to the patentee; consider whether defendant's mingling was culpable or obstructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement that causes sales may justify recovery of entire profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the device of the patent may be a mere improvement on an existing device, the improvement may nevertheless be the thing which brings about the sale and if that is the case, the plaintiff is entitled to recover the entire profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patented improvement is the effective sales driver for the unitary product, recover full profits rather than a partial apportionment; analyze causal contribution to demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of ascertaining cost: direct evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking an account of profits in the method indicated, it is generally easy to ascertain the amount which the defendant realized for the articles which he made and sold; but it is generally difficult to determine how much it cost him to make and sell them. Such an inquiry must consist of collecting direct evidence upon the subject; and cannot consist in ascertaining the cost to other parties of making and selling similar articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require direct, defendant-specific cost evidence (materials, labor, overhead allocations). Do not rely on third-party cost estimates. The elements allowed to enter into cost include the market value of materials on hand at the time the infringement began and the actual cost of materials subsequently purchased (but not the market value of the latter at time they were used).
